prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 regime
for the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube detector, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the one candidate on which nearly the whole committee converges: five of seven rankers place it, two put it first, and the two-name credit (Katori for the magic-wavelength lattice scheme, Ye for driving it to record accuracy and stability) is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. It is independently reproduced at the 10^-18 level in many national laboratories and is tied to the pending redefinition of the second, so it is mature as well as original. Neutrino astronomy is a different kind of achievement, a new observational window opened by an instrument. IceCube detected the diffuse TeV-PeV astrophysical neutrino flux in 2013, and this was followed by the 2018 TXS 0506+056 association, the NGC 1068 evidence and the Galactic-plane result. Together these give a measurement, a detector and a physical consequence (cosmic-ray accelerators are now observable through neutrinos) that are independent of any model of the sources. Pairing a precision-measurement advance with a discovery in astroparticle physics gives two distinct achievements within the three-person limit and spreads the prize across fields without diluting either citation.
statement.case_against: My opening rank for IceCube is the weakest-supported part of this proposal: only Danielsson ranks it besides me, and a one-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds is hard to defend. Halzen is the driving proponent and long-time leader, but the AMANDA precursor, the detector construction and the analysis teams that found the flux were decisive, and the supplied credit list offers no second or third name. If the committee cannot justify a single laureate, the astroparticle part falls away and the clock stands alone. Separately, topological insulators (B028) have more first-place votes than any other candidate, and the sheer breadth of support there means that a prize omitting them may look like an arbitrary choice. I also acknowledge that a combined prize puts two thinly connected subjects together, and that the three-person cap works against a three-name B028 or B046 being paired with anything else.

responses.point: Ranks topological insulators first, with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan as the laureates, arguing that the prediction, HgTe realisation and 3D ARPES identification form a chain from idea to observation, and also ranks IceCube second as a discovery-centred case.
responses.response: I agree that B028 is a central and overdue discovery, and your ranking of IceCube second is the only support I have for the neutrino part, so I take it seriously. We differ on the credit. Omitting Mele is hard to defend when Kane and Mele co-authored the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal, while Hasan's experimental claim sits on a different branch from the theory-plus-HgTe line. A three-person B028 forces us either to leave out a co-originator or to leave out the 3D experiments. I would rather keep B028 as my first alternative than build the prize around a configuration whose attribution is contested inside the credited names.

responses.point: Ranks the optical lattice clock first, noting that Katori's proposal and Ye's JILA realisation are the two decisive strands, and flags his own links to the Hall-lab environment as a potential connection.
responses.response: I agree that the clock attribution is the cleanest on the list and that timing is good. I would add that Hall and Hänsch were recognised for the comb in 2005, so the new prize is a successor and not a repeat, but your remark about Ye and the Hall environment should be handled openly: it is a personal connection that you should declare for the committee to weigh. I would not discount the science for it, since the credit argument stands on the published record. Where I differ slightly is that I would not rule out other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat); the two-name cap is a choice we should be able to defend to outside readers.

responses.point: Ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first because a theoretical flat-band prediction preceded and guided a field-defining experiment, and proposes MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei.
responses.response: The prediction-then-experiment structure is a real strength, and I ranked B046 fourth myself. My reservations are maturity and credit. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the main experiments are about eight years old, so I judge this somewhat early, which is not a weakness of the physics. On credit, Andrei's STM evidence and Bistritzer's share of the 2011 theory are both real claims, and a three-person limit cuts one of them. I would keep B046 as a strong second alternative, and I would revisit it in a later cycle once the pairing mechanism is clearer.

responses.point: Ranks the optical lattice clock first from the standpoint of atomic structure and light-shift control, calling the two-name configuration fair, and ranks the theta13 measurement fourth, noting that the Daya Bay and T2K names omit RENO and Double Chooz.
responses.response: I share your view of the clock and value that you read it as an atomic-structure achievement and not only as a metrology success. On theta13 we are close, since I ranked it fifth for the same attribution reason: three spokespersons cannot stand for four collaborations, and the 2015 oscillation prize already covers the main discovery. I would not put B002 into the preferred configuration for that reason, but if the committee wants a second particle or astroparticle part, I would ask you whether the neutrino-astronomy case looks stronger or weaker to you than theta13 on the credit question.

uncertainties: Whether a single-name credit for Halzen is defensible for the IceCube discovery given the size of the collaboration and the absence of other credited names.
Whether the committee prefers a single-achievement prize for the clock, a three-person topological-insulator prize, or the two-part combination I propose.
Whether other lattice-clock groups have credit claims strong enough to alter the Katori and Ye pairing.
The maturity of source identification in neutrino astronomy: the diffuse flux is established, but the NGC 1068 and Galactic-plane results are still developing.
statement.conflict_note: No specific recusal issue is apparent from my profile for B034, B028, B046 or B002. My documented work is in space and balloon instrumentation and gamma-ray polarimetry (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur, a proposed gamma-ray burst polarimeter), and no IceCube link is recorded. The gamma-ray burst afterglow candidate (B004) is adjacent to my gamma-ray burst instrumentation interests, which is a field proximity that should be noted, and I would not take a lead role on that candidate.
